fr: Le marché est ouvert le samedi matin.
en: The market is open on Saturday morning.
notes: Liaison between est and ouvert adds a t sound that is not heard when est stands alone.

fr: J'achète des pommes rouges.
en: I buy red apples.
notes: Je elides to j' before the vowel-initial verb achète.

fr: Elle choisit des tomates bien mûres.
en: She chooses ripe tomatoes.
notes: The final t in choisit is silent, easy to forget when writing.

fr: Le vendeur pèse les fraises.
en: The seller weighs the strawberries.
notes: Pèse needs a grave accent to mark the open e sound, a detail invisible in casual speech.

fr: Combien coûte ce fromage ?
en: How much does this cheese cost?
notes: Combien contains two nasal vowels that are easy to under-articulate when writing quickly.

fr: Les légumes sont frais aujourd'hui.
en: The vegetables are fresh today.
notes: Sont sounds like son; only the verb context tells you to add the final t.

fr: Il vend des poissons frais.
en: He sells fresh fish.
notes: The final d of vend is silent, a common trap for this regular verb ending.

fr: Nous cherchons des fleurs jaunes.
en: We are looking for yellow flowers.
notes: Jaunes agrees in gender and number with fleurs, adding a silent final s.

fr: Vous voulez un kilo de carottes ?
en: Do you want a kilo of carrots?
notes: The unstressed e in de is a schwa that can fade in speech but must stay in writing.

fr: Ils achètent du pain à la boulangerie.
en: They buy bread at the bakery.
notes: Liaison between ils and achètent produces a z sound signaling the plural, not audible in il achète.

fr: Elles regardent les fruits exotiques.
en: They look at the exotic fruits.
notes: The verb ending -ent in regardent is silent, so elle regarde and elles regardent sound almost identical.

fr: Je prends deux kilos de pommes de terre.
en: I am taking two kilos of potatoes.
ipa: /ʒə pʁɑ̃ dø ki.lo də pɔm də tɛʁ/
notes: The final ds in prends is silent, a common trap when writing present-tense verb forms.

fr: Le marchand rend la monnaie rapidement.
en: The merchant gives back the change quickly.
notes: Marchand, rend, and rapidement all contain nasal vowels that are easy to under-articulate when writing.

fr: Cette pastèque est très lourde.
en: This watermelon is very heavy.
notes: Lourde adds a feminine final e to agree with pastèque, a change not heard in speech.

fr: Les abricots sont chers cette semaine.
en: Apricots are expensive this week.
notes: Liaison between les and abricots adds a z sound marking the plural.

fr: On paie en espèces ou par carte.
en: We pay in cash or by card.
notes: Ou (or) has no accent, unlike its homophone où (where); context decides the spelling.

fr: Le client demande le prix des oranges.
en: The customer asks the price of the oranges.
ipa: /lə kli.jɑ̃ də.mɑ̃d lə pʁi de ɔ.ʁɑ̃ʒ/
notes: The final t in client is silent, a frequent spelling slip in dictée.

fr: La marchande sourit à ses clients.
en: The market woman smiles at her customers.
notes: À needs a grave accent to distinguish it from a (has), even though they sound the same.

fr: Les enfants aiment les fraises sucrées.
en: The children love sweet strawberries.
notes: Liaison between les and enfants adds a z that signals the plural article.

fr: Il y a beaucoup de monde au marché.
en: There are a lot of people at the market.
notes: The nasal vowel in monde is easy to under-pronounce, leading learners to drop the n when writing.

fr: Les pommes sont dans le panier.
en: The apples are in the basket.
notes: Dans ends in a nasal vowel that can be confused in spelling with dent or dents.

fr: Elle porte un grand sac de courses.
en: She is carrying a big shopping bag.
ipa: /ɛl pɔʁt œ̃ gʁɑ̃ sak də kuʁs/
notes: The final d of grand is silent before a consonant, unlike in liaison contexts.

fr: Le poissonnier nettoie les poissons.
en: The fishmonger cleans the fish.
notes: Poissonnier doubles the n, a spelling detail not obvious from pronunciation.

fr: Nous achetons du fromage de chèvre.
en: We are buying goat cheese.
notes: Liaison links nous and achetons with a z sound absent from the written words individually.

fr: Les fleurs sentent très bon.
en: The flowers smell very good.
notes: The -ent ending of sentent is silent, matching the plural subject without being heard.

fr: Je voudrais un kilo de cerises.
en: I would like a kilo of cherries.
notes: The schwa in je and de often disappears in fast speech but must remain in writing.

fr: Le fromager coupe une tranche de fromage.
en: The cheesemonger cuts a slice of cheese.
ipa: /lə fʁɔ.ma.ʒe kup yn tʁɑ̃ʃ də fʁɔ.maʒ/
notes: The -er ending of fromager is pronounced like é, a classic dictée confusion point.

fr: Les clients font la queue devant l'étal.
en: The customers wait in line in front of the stall.
ipa: /le kli.jɑ̃ fɔ̃ la kø də.vɑ̃ le.tal/
notes: Le étal elides to l'étal before the vowel-initial noun.

fr: Elle met les légumes dans son sac.
en: She puts the vegetables in her bag.
ipa: /ɛl mɛ le le.gym dɑ̃ sɔ̃ sak/
notes: Son (her) sounds identical to sont (are), so only meaning distinguishes the spelling.

fr: Le vendeur crie les prix du jour.
en: The seller calls out the day's prices.
ipa: /lə vɑ̃.dœʁ kʁi le pʁi dy ʒuʁ/
notes: The final x in prix is silent, easy to omit or misplace in dictée.

fr: Nous goûtons les olives noires.
en: We taste the black olives.
notes: The circumflex on goûtons is silent but required in spelling, marking a lost historical s.

fr: Ils vendent des herbes fraîches.
en: They sell fresh herbs.
notes: Vendent carries a nasal vowel followed by a silent -ent ending, both easy to misspell.

fr: La salade coûte deux euros.
en: The salad costs two euros.
notes: Liaison between deux and euros adds a z sound not present when deux stands alone.

fr: Ce raisin vient du sud de la France.
en: This grape comes from the south of France.
ipa: /sə ʁɛ.zɛ̃ vjɛ̃ dy syd də la fʁɑ̃s/
notes: Raisin ends in a nasal vowel that beginners often spell with an extra n.

fr: Les prix affichés sont clairs.
en: The displayed prices are clear.
notes: Liaison after prix surfaces a z sound that the silent written x does not suggest.

fr: Elle achète six œufs frais.
en: She buys six fresh eggs.
notes: Œufs in the plural loses the f sound heard in singular œuf, an irregular spelling-to-sound trap.

fr: Le boucher prépare la viande.
en: The butcher prepares the meat.
notes: The final r of boucher is silent, following the standard -er ending pattern.

fr: Nous choisissons un bon melon.
en: We are choosing a good melon.
notes: Un, bon, and melon all contain nasal vowels that are easy to under-articulate in dictée.

fr: Les asperges sont vertes et fines.
en: The asparagus are green and thin.
notes: Vertes and fines both add silent feminine plural endings to agree with asperges.

fr: Le marché ferme à treize heures.
en: The market closes at one o'clock.
notes: À carries an accent grave to distinguish it from a, though both are pronounced the same.

fr: J'aime l'odeur du pain frais.
en: I love the smell of fresh bread.
notes: Both je and le elide before vowel-initial words, giving j'aime and l'odeur.

fr: Elle porte des sacs très lourds.
en: She is carrying very heavy bags.
notes: The final ds in lourds is completely silent, only visible in the written plural form.

fr: Les touristes visitent le marché local.
en: The tourists visit the local market.
notes: The silent -ent ending on visitent shows the plural subject without any audible change.

fr: Le vieux marchand connaît tous ses clients.
en: The old merchant knows all his customers.
ipa: /lə vjø maʁ.ʃɑ̃ kɔ.nɛ tu se kli.jɑ̃/
notes: Connaît keeps a circumflex accent on the i, a silent mark that must not be forgotten.

fr: Nous prenons un citron et deux oranges.
en: We are taking a lemon and two oranges.
notes: Citron ends in a nasal vowel often mis-transcribed with an extra n.

fr: Les champignons sont dans une petite boîte.
en: The mushrooms are in a small box.
notes: Boîte keeps a circumflex on the i, a silent accent that changes nothing in pronunciation but is required in spelling.

fr: Elle achète des épices pour la soupe.
en: She buys spices for the soup.
notes: Liaison between des and épices produces an audible z marking the plural.

fr: Le marché est près de l'église.
en: The market is near the church.
notes: La église elides to l'église because the noun begins with a vowel sound.

fr: Ils goûtent le miel local.
en: They taste the local honey.
notes: The silent -ent ending on goûtent signals a plural subject that cannot be heard.

fr: La marchande pèse les pommes une à une.
en: The market woman weighs the apples one by one.
ipa: /la maʁ.ʃɑ̃d pɛz le pɔm yn a yn/
notes: À needs its accent grave even though it sounds exactly like a (has).

fr: Les clients paient et partent vite.
en: The customers pay and leave quickly.
notes: Et (and) is a homophone of est (is); only the sentence meaning tells you which to write.

fr: Hier, j'ai acheté des fraises au marché.
en: Yesterday, I bought strawberries at the market.
ipa: /jɛʁ ʒe aʃ.te de fʁɛz o maʁ.ʃe/
notes: Acheté ends in a sound identical to acheter and achetez, so the ending must be chosen by grammar, not sound.

fr: Nous avons choisi les meilleurs fromages.
en: We chose the best cheeses.
notes: Liaison between nous and avons adds a z sound not visible in either word alone.

fr: Elle a payé avec sa carte bancaire.
en: She paid with her bank card.
ipa: /ɛl a pɛ.je a.vɛk sa kaʁt bɑ̃.kɛʁ/
notes: Payé sounds the same as payer and payez, so the past participle ending relies on grammar, not sound.

fr: Ils sont allés au marché tôt le matin.
en: They went to the market early in the morning.
ipa: /il sɔ̃ a.le o maʁ.ʃe to lə ma.tɛ̃/
notes: Allés takes a silent plural s to agree with ils because it uses the auxiliary être.

fr: Le vendeur a pesé les tomates.
en: The seller weighed the tomatoes.
notes: Pesé ends in the same sound as peser, a frequent past participle confusion.

fr: Nous allons acheter du pain demain.
en: We are going to buy bread tomorrow.
notes: Liaison between nous and allons produces a z sound that signals the plural subject.

fr: Elle va goûter le fromage de chèvre.
en: She is going to taste the goat cheese.
ipa: /ɛl va gu.te lə fʁɔ.maʒ də ʃɛvʁ/
notes: The circumflex on goûter is silent but must be written, marking a historical lost s.

fr: Vous avez trouvé des fruits mûrs.
en: You found ripe fruits.
notes: Trouvé sounds identical to trouver and trouvez, so only grammar tells you which ending to write.

fr: Les enfants ont mangé toutes les cerises.
en: The children ate all the cherries.
notes: Ont (have) is a homophone of on (one), distinguished only by grammatical context.

fr: On a acheté beaucoup de légumes.
en: We bought a lot of vegetables.
notes: On sounds like ont, so writers must rely on meaning to choose the right spelling.

fr: Où as-tu trouvé ces belles fleurs ?
en: Where did you find these beautiful flowers?
ipa: /u a ty tʁu.ve se bɛl flœʁ/
notes: Où (where) carries an accent to distinguish it from ou (or), though both sound identical.

fr: Elle a demandé le prix des poires.
en: She asked the price of the pears.
ipa: /ɛl a də.mɑ̃.de lə pʁi de pwaʁ/
notes: Demandé ends the same as demander, a common past participle spelling trap.

fr: Nous avons marché longtemps entre les étals.
en: We walked for a long time between the stalls.
notes: Longtemps contains two nasal vowels and a silent final s, easy to misspell.

fr: Ils ont goûté les olives avant d'acheter.
en: They tasted the olives before buying.
notes: De acheter elides to d'acheter before the vowel-initial verb.

fr: Le marchand a donné la monnaie à Paul.
en: The merchant gave the change to Paul.
ipa: /lə maʁ.ʃɑ̃ a dɔ.ne la mɔ.nɛ a pɔl/
notes: The sentence contains both a (has) and à (to), which sound identical but are spelled differently.

fr: Elle a pris deux kilos de pommes.
en: She took two kilos of apples.
ipa: /ɛl a pʁi dø ki.lo də pɔm/
notes: The final s of the past participle pris is silent, easy to drop in dictée.

fr: On va négocier le prix du poisson.
en: We are going to negotiate the price of the fish.
ipa: /ɔ̃ va ne.gɔ.sje lə pʁi dy pwa.sɔ̃/
notes: On and poisson both carry nasal vowels that beginners often under-pronounce when writing.

fr: Les clients ont fait la queue longtemps.
en: The customers waited in line for a long time.
ipa: /le kli.jɑ̃ ɔ̃ fɛ la kø lɔ̃.tɑ̃/
notes: Ont (have) must not be confused with its homophone on (one), a frequent dictée error.

fr: Il a vendu tous ses légumes ce matin.
en: He sold all his vegetables this morning.
ipa: /il a vɑ̃.dy tu se le.gym sə ma.tɛ̃/
notes: The final s of tous is silent before a consonant, unlike when it stands alone as a pronoun.

fr: Nous avons mis les fruits dans un sac.
en: We put the fruits in a bag.
notes: Dans and un both end in nasal vowels that liaison links with a z sound.

fr: Elle est arrivée tôt pour choisir les meilleurs produits.
en: She arrived early to choose the best products.
ipa: /ɛl ɛ.t‿a.ʁi.ve to puʁ ʃwa.ziʁ le mɛ.jœʁ pʁɔ.dɥi/
notes: Arrivée takes a silent feminine e to agree with elle since it uses the auxiliary être.

fr: Ils vont vendre des fleurs demain matin.
en: They are going to sell flowers tomorrow morning.
ipa: /il vɔ̃ vɑ̃dʁ de flœʁ də.mɛ̃ ma.tɛ̃/
notes: Vont ends in a nasal vowel and a silent t, distinct from words it merely resembles in speech.

fr: On a payé en espèces au marchand.
en: We paid in cash to the merchant.
notes: Payé sounds like payer, so the correct ending depends on recognizing the past participle form.

fr: Le boulanger a préparé du pain frais.
en: The baker prepared fresh bread.
ipa: /lə bu.lɑ̃.ʒe a pʁe.pa.ʁe dy pɛ̃ fʁɛ/
notes: Préparé ends the same as préparer, requiring grammatical knowledge to spell correctly.

fr: Nous avons acheté du miel et des épices.
en: We bought honey and spices.
notes: Et (and) is a homophone of est (is), so context alone determines the correct spelling.

fr: Elle a comparé les prix entre deux étals.
en: She compared the prices between two stalls.
ipa: /ɛl a kɔ̃.pa.ʁe le pʁi ɑ̃.tʁə dø.z‿e.tal/
notes: Comparé sounds identical to comparer, another past-participle spelling trap.

fr: Ont-ils trouvé un bon fromager ?
en: Did they find a good cheesemonger?
notes: In this inverted question, ont must not be confused with its homophone on despite sounding alike.

fr: Le fromager a coupé une belle tranche.
en: The cheesemonger cut a nice slice.
ipa: /lə fʁɔ.ma.ʒe a ku.pe yn bɛl tʁɑ̃ʃ/
notes: Coupé ends the same as couper, a classic past participle versus infinitive confusion.

fr: Nous sommes passés devant le marché aux fleurs.
en: We passed by the flower market.
ipa: /nu sɔm pa.se də.vɑ̃ lə maʁ.ʃe o flœʁ/
notes: Passés adds a silent plural s to agree with the subject because it uses the auxiliary être.

fr: Elle a choisi de belles poires vertes.
en: She chose some nice green pears.
ipa: /ɛl a ʃwa.zi də bɛl pwaʁ vɛʁt/
notes: The past participle choisi ends in a silent i sound with no audible final consonant to guide spelling.

fr: Ils ont vendu leurs légumes très vite.
en: They sold their vegetables very quickly.
notes: Ont must be distinguished from its homophone on through the plural subject ils.

fr: On va acheter des asperges fraîches.
en: We are going to buy fresh asparagus.
notes: Liaison between des and asperges adds an audible z that marks the plural.

fr: Le marchand a baissé le prix des oranges.
en: The merchant lowered the price of the oranges.
ipa: /lə maʁ.ʃɑ̃ a bɛ.se lə pʁi de.z‿ɔ.ʁɑ̃ʒ/
notes: Baissé sounds the same as baisser, requiring the past participle ending to be chosen by grammar.

fr: Nous avons rapporté des légumes du marché.
en: We brought back vegetables from the market.
notes: Rapporté ends in the same sound as rapporter, another present infinitive versus past participle trap.
